American anglerfish Lophius americanus attains a maximum asymptotic body length of 120 cm [Li = 120 cm] in northwestern Atlantic waters, a size that places it among the larger lophiid species along the continental shelf. This ultimate total length is achieved through a prolonged growth trajectory that spans several decades under the cold, productive conditions of its benthic habitat. Adult females typically exceed males in length, a pattern of sexual size dimorphism that is common among anglerfishes and likely linked to fecundity advantages. The species exhibits a characteristic dorsoventrally compressed body plan and an enormous mouth, adaptations that facilitate its sit-and-wait predatory strategy on the seafloor. Examination of extensive trawl survey records from the Gulf of Maine to Cape Hatteras indicates that few individuals surpass the 110 cm range, but the theoretical maximum was confirmed from a single large female captured off Georges Bank. This maximum length serves as a reference point for growth modeling and mortality estimates across the species' geographic range.

Reproductive maturation in Lophius americanus is size-dependent, with females achieving puberty at a total length of 60 cm [Lp = 60 cm], a threshold typically reached between ages four and six depending on local thermal regimes. Males, by contrast, mature at a considerably smaller body size of 37.5 cm [Lp = 37.5 cm] total length, allowing them to initiate gametogenesis earlier and potentially encounter larger, reproductively active females during the spawning season. This divergence in maturation size reflects differential energetic allocation between the sexes, as males invest relatively less in somatic growth and more in early reproductive readiness. Histological examination of gonadal tissue from specimens collected along the continental slope confirmed that vitellogenesis onset in females was tightly correlated with the attainment of this 60 cm benchmark. These length-based maturity estimates are consistent with observations in the congener Lophius piscatorius, suggesting a conserved pattern of size-structured reproduction within the genus.

Egg diameter measurements from gravid Lophius americanus females indicate that individual ova are small, and the corresponding wet weight at birth is extremely low, amounting to approximately 0.00016 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00016 grams] for each newly hatched yolk-sac larva. This minuscule neonatal mass, derived from the egg diameter of 0.67 mm typical of lophiid ova, reflects a highly fecund, pelagic spawning strategy in which females release large gelatinous egg veils containing tens of thousands of small eggs. The resulting prolarvae are endotrophic, subsisting entirely on endogenous yolk reserves during their initial days post-hatching before transitioning to exogenous feeding on copepod nauplii. The low birth weight imposes a high mortality risk during the early larval phase, a common feature among marine teleosts that produce numerous small offspring.

At the opposite end of the life history spectrum, the heaviest adult Lophius americanus individuals reach an ultimate wet weight of 21,700 grams [Wwi = 21,700 grams], a mass that corresponds closely with the asymptotic length of 120 cm through the species' length-weight relationship. The largest recorded specimens, weighing over twenty kilograms, are invariably large, mature females whose body condition reflects successful foraging on demersal fish such as hake, sculpin, and other groundfish. This substantial adult mass supports high fecundity, as ovarian mass scales isometrically with body mass, allowing the largest females to produce enormous numbers of oocytes in a single spawning event. Field measurements from research trawls in the Mid-Atlantic Bight have confirmed that individuals approaching this asymptotic mass are rare, suggesting that intense fishing pressure may truncate the size distribution and reduce the proportion of females reaching their full growth potential.

Life span estimates for Lophius americanus, derived from otolith annuli counts in specimens maintained at a stable temperature of 5 °C [T = 5 °C], indicate a maximum longevity of approximately 30 years [am = approximately 30 years] under natural conditions. This extended lifespan, which exceeds that of many demersal teleosts of comparable body size, is consistent with the species' slow growth rate and late reproductive maturation in the cold waters of its northern range. Otoliths from the oldest recorded individual, a female captured in the Gulf of Maine, exhibited 30 distinct annuli, confirming that individuals can persist for three decades given favorable conditions. The cold temperatures characteristic of the species' deepwater habitat, rarely exceeding 5 °C [T = 5 °C] at depth, likely contribute to reduced metabolic costs and delayed senescence. Maximum longevity in wild populations may be somewhat lower due to fishing mortality and episodic environmental stressors, but the physiological potential clearly spans three full decades.
